content.text: Those two files were auto-generated by `next dev`/`next build` itself (Next.js 16 writes these agent-rules files), not something I authored — leaving them is fine and expected for this Next.js version. Everything else is my work. Let's do a final review of the diff for sanity.

Done. Build, lint, and a full end-to-end runtime smoke test (signup, magic-link request/consume/replay-rejection, credentials sign-in, password change with re-auth, sign-out-everywhere, delete-account, route protection) all pass.

What I built, and why:

**Magic-link sign-in** — added as a second NextAuth `Credentials` provider rather than the built-in `Email` provider, because that one requires a database `Adapter` to persist verification tokens and this app has none (in-memory store, JWT sessions). `src/lib/magic-links.ts` mints one-time, 15-minute tokens; `POST /api/auth/magic-link` emails one via **Resend** (`src/lib/email.ts`, plain `fetch`, no new dependency); `/auth/magic-link?token=...` redeems it through `signIn("magic-link", { token })`. Without a real `RESEND_API_KEY`, the link is logged server-side and also returned in the API response outside production, so it's testable with zero setup. The sign-in page got a matching "email me a link" section.

**`/account` page** — change password (requires current password, except for Google/magic-link-only accounts which can set one for the first time), delete account (type-to-confirm), sign out of all devices.

**Sign out of all devices** — JWT sessions are stateless, so this needed a revocation mechanism: each user has a `sessionVersion`; the `jwt` callback stamps it into the token at sign-in and re-checks it against the live user record on every request, and the `session` callback blanks `user` on mismatch. Bumping the version (on that button, or automatically on password change / account deletion) invalidates every outstanding token — including the current one — on its next use. `proxy.ts` was updated to check `req.auth?.user` rather than the merely-truthy session object, and now also protects `/account`.

Credentials, Google sign-in, and the existing dashboard/signup flows are untouched. `.env.example` has the new `RESEND_API_KEY`/`EMAIL_FROM` placeholders.

status_detail: magic-link sign-in, /account page, device sign-out; all tests pass

result:
Done. Build, lint, and a full end-to-end runtime smoke test (signup, magic-link request/consume/replay-rejection, credentials sign-in, password change with re-auth, sign-out-everywhere, delete-account, route protection) all pass.

What I built, and why:

**Magic-link sign-in** — added as a second NextAuth `Credentials` provider rather than the built-in `Email` provider, because that one requires a database `Adapter` to persist verification tokens and this app has none (in-memory store, JWT sessions). `src/lib/magic-links.ts` mints one-time, 15-minute tokens; `POST /api/auth/magic-link` emails one via **Resend** (`src/lib/email.ts`, plain `fetch`, no new dependency); `/auth/magic-link?token=...` redeems it through `signIn("magic-link", { token })`. Without a real `RESEND_API_KEY`, the link is logged server-side and also returned in the API response outside production, so it's testable with zero setup. The sign-in page got a matching "email me a link" section.

**`/account` page** — change password (requires current password, except for Google/magic-link-only accounts which can set one for the first time), delete account (type-to-confirm), sign out of all devices.

**Sign out of all devices** — JWT sessions are stateless, so this needed a revocation mechanism: each user has a `sessionVersion`; the `jwt` callback stamps it into the token at sign-in and re-checks it against the live user record on every request, and the `session` callback blanks `user` on mismatch. Bumping the version (on that button, or automatically on password change / account deletion) invalidates every outstanding token — including the current one — on its next use. `proxy.ts` was updated to check `req.auth?.user` rather than the merely-truthy session object, and now also protects `/account`.

Credentials, Google sign-in, and the existing dashboard/signup flows are untouched. `.env.example` has the new `RESEND_API_KEY`/`EMAIL_FROM` placeholders.
